entries.title: You Have Mail: Set-Theoretic Types for Actors
entries.abstract: We present a type system for the processes of Elixir, a dynamic language based on the actor model whose static type system covers only its functional core. Each process is typed by pid(t), where the “interface” t is the type of the messages the process expects in its mailbox: sends are checked against the recipient's interface, and receives rely on the interface of the process that performs them. One of the difficulties of typing Elixir is that mailboxes are implicit: a function shipped in a message may evaluate self() and execute receive instructions, and both refer to whichever process eventually runs the function—self() returns that process's pid, receive reads that process's mailbox—so the mailbox they act on is not known where the function is written. We solve this problem by inferring, for every function, bounds on the type of the mailboxes it can be used with; as a result, the system types higher-order functions that travel in messages even when they contain reference to self() and receive instructions. The only new annotation the programmer writes is the interface of each spawned process; everything else is inferred by reusing the existing subtyping and constraint-resolution machinery of Elixir, and the system is proved sound. For legacy code, the interface can be reconstructed from the receive clauses: what the branches do with their messages bounds it from above, and the most permissive solution is sharp enough to recover received pids and closures.

entries.title: Hereditary permutations for simple types revisited: A baby case for University Algebra
entries.abstract: It is a classical result that the definable isomorphisms of the simply typed lambda-calculus with function types are exactly the hereditary permutations, and that they are generated by A →B →C ≅B →A →C and congruence. We give a new proof of this result that stays inside beta-normal eta-long typed terms and uses no completeness theorem: an induction that descends through both components of an isomorphism at once. We then go one level up and prove a coherence theorem: two derivations of an isomorphism denote the same isomorphism if and only if they are equal modulo an explicit list of equations (groupoid laws, functoriality, involution, naturality and the braid equation), so these equations present the groupoid of isomorphisms, a hereditary version of the Coxeter presentation of the symmetric groups. All results are formalised in Agda, on intrinsically typed syntax with hereditary substitution, without postulates. The work is a case study for the syntactic completeness conjecture of University Algebra, a proposed solution of Tarski's high school algebra problem using dependent types, whose semantic counterpart is open. We explain the motivation and which parts of the method we expect to carry over.

entries.title: On the semantics of conditional branching
entries.abstract: Motivated by the non-standard interpretations of if-then-else in probabilistic and quantum programs we review the different semantics of conditional branching and propose a unifying categorical structure for the interpretation of if-then-else. We show that many semantically important categories possess this structure, covering inter alia classical, probabilistic, quantum or non-deterministic computations. We examine algebraic structures related to and generated by this categorical structure, in particular on collections of predicates. In this setting we show that the skew-associativity rules of GKATs and barycentric algebras are two instances of a common skew-associativity rule.

entries.title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
entries.abstract: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool, Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction α of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at α = 1%, it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline, and still 43.8-60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.

entries.title: Tenon: A Unified Programming Framework for Retargetable PIM Compilation
entries.abstract: Processing-in-memory (PIM) is emerging as a building block of heterogeneous systems for memory-bound workloads, and commercial prototypes now span near-bank SIMD engines, bank-level GDDR accelerators, programmable DRAM cores, and bit-level in-SRAM processors. Their programming stacks are fragmented: no abstraction or compiler is shared across vendors, and per-device models range from instruction sequences to C-like languages. Data layout further complicates the problem: tight compute-memory integration makes data layout a first-order optimization, yet existing PIM compilers lack a unified way to represent and optimize it. A key observation is that PIM compilation targets can be modeled as nested grids of compute and storage units connected by legal data-transfer paths. We present Tenon, a unified programming framework for retargetable PIM compilation. It decouples workload, compilation target, and cost specifications, so a workload is expressed once and compiled through a unified programming framework. Tenon generalizes the F₂ linear layout algebra from GPU compilers to map logical work and data onto these compute and storage grids. It automatically constructs a minimum-movement data layout given a workload and a target specification. We evaluate Tenon on six PIM backends: five commercial backends and AttAcc, a state-of-the-art academic HBM-based PIM architecture. Across the commercial backends, it matches or outperforms vendor, expert, and compiler baselines, with geometric-mean speedups of up to 1.20× and individual speedups up to 3.65×. For end-to-end GPT-13B decoding on AttAcc, Tenon-compiled workloads run 1.2–1.3% faster than those compiled by DCC, a state-of-the-art PIM compiler, across all three batch-4 configurations. Together, these results demonstrate Tenon's performance portability across diverse PIM target families.

entries.title: A Principled Approach to Concurrency, Nondeterminism, and Asynchrony in Choreographies
entries.abstract: Choreographic programming (CP) describes a distributed system as a global program and compiles it into communicating network programs via endpoint projection (EPP). Asynchrony captures the independent progress of communicating processes, while nondeterminism captures the range of behaviours that can arise from their interactions. However, the integration of both features into a theory of CP is absent. We present Nyarlathotep, the first asynchronous nondeterministic CP framework. We define its operational semantics of choreographies and networks using labelled transition systems. Besides asynchrony and choreographic nondeterminism, Nyarlathotep supports expressive features including general branching, out-of-order execution, and general recursion with parameterised procedures that processes can enter independently. We prove EPP sound and complete, establishing strong behavioural equivalence between the semantics of choreographies and their projected networks. We prove that projected networks are communication-safe and deadlock-free. We mechanised all our results in Lean 4.

entries.title: Matching-Logic-Based Understanding of Polynomial Functors and their Initial/Final Models Revisited
entries.abstract: Many data types used in programming are initial algebras or final coalgebras of polynomial functors. We show how to specify them uniformly in matching logic, using the representation of polynomial functors as unary container functors X↦Σ_(a:A)X^(B[a]). For each container functor, we give a matching logic theory of its initial algebra and one of its final coalgebra. Besides the no-junk and no-confusion axioms and their duals, these theories include axioms about the elements that represent functions, for the initial algebra, and a bisimilarity axiom and a realisation axiom, for the final coalgebra; the existence axioms use free set variables to range over all subsets of a model. We prove that, in every model, the algebra extracted from the model is an initial algebra (a W-type) and the extracted coalgebra is a final coalgebra (an M-type) of the container extracted from the model, i.e., the one given by the model's interpretation of the shapes and positions, and that such models exist. So the data types are captured relative to the interpretation of the sorts of shapes and positions, and absolutely whenever these sorts are fixed by auxiliary specifications, which we show for finite sets, products, dependent sums, and (co)inductive sorts built from them. We derive the induction, coinduction, and bisimulation principles as theorems, and illustrate the approach on lists and on Moore machines. This paper revises and substantially extends a paper published in EPTCS 389 (FROM 2023): several axioms are corrected, and the adequacy and satisfiability proofs are new.
entries.comment: 44 pages. Revised and substantially extended version of arXiv:2309.13798 (EPTCS 389, FROM 2023); Appendix C lists the changes

entries.title: Stephen: Verifying Sequencer-Aided Coordination Systems with Cross-View Prophecy
entries.abstract: Many distributed systems achieve high performance by relying on dedicated sequencers to order requests, leaving replicas to commit them in that order. Despite more than a decade of such sequencer-aided coordination (SAC) systems, from Corfu and NOPaxos to LazyLog and SwitchBFT, their correctness has been argued only with pen-and-paper proofs or bounded model checking at the protocol level. In this paper, we formally verify implementations of SAC protocols. The sequencer seems to make this easy: it decides the order of all requests, so the proof can place each request's linearization point at the sequencer using a well-known technique, prophecy variables. Yet a linearization point placed at the sequencer is not durable, because the sequencer orders a request before any replica commits it. Crashes and other rare events may trigger a view change that discards the request, nullifying the earlier decision and the proof that rests on it. Our framework, Stephen, extends prophecy variables to handle view changes, and we make three contributions. (1) We develop cross-view prophecy peek, which lets the proof follow a request across view changes until it is either committed or permanently discarded. (2) Our verification uncovered bugs in existing SAC implementations, including one that can lose committed requests. We fix them and prove the fixes correct. (3) We apply Stephen to NOPaxos, Corfu and LazyLog. We build verified implementations with machine-checked proofs of linearizability. They perform within 17% of their open-source, unverified counterparts. The verified implementations and proofs will be open-sourced.

entries.title: Validating Concurrent Correctness Witnesses with Ghosts by Thread-Modular Abstract Interpretation
entries.abstract: Concurrent programs are notoriously difficult to write and to reason about, and even tools based on sound theoretical foundations can produce incorrect results due to implementation bugs. Correctness witnesses have been proposed as a way to increase the confidence in the verdicts of software verifiers by enabling independent validation. Recently, correctness witnesses have been extended to the concurrent setting, by introducing ghost variables to allow encoding more expressive invariants. While different approaches to producing witnesses with ghosts exist, validation techniques are still lacking; instead of leveraging the information encoded in the ghosts to guide the validation process, validators merely treat ghost instrumentation and invariants over ghost variables as additional proof obligations. We propose a novel framework for the validation of concurrent correctness witnesses that exploits the semantic information encoded in ghost variables. It combines a checking phase, which establishes the semantic content of the ghost instrumentation, with an exploitation phase making use of this information. Both phases are formulated as thread-modular abstract interpretation. In particular, we consider two different classes of ghost variables and techniques for exploiting them, one based on resource invariants and one based on phases. Phase ghosts guide the degree to which the abstract interpretation considers interleavings instead of always abstracting them coarsely. In this way, the abstract interpreter can validate witnesses containing invariants beyond the reach of unguided thread-modular analysis, while still retaining its scalability benefits. We have implemented our framework in a static analyzer and evaluate it on witnesses encoding resource invariants obtained from a state-of-the-art software verifier, as well as on hand-crafted witnesses encoding phase information.
entries.comment: Accepted to POPL '27; Extended version with appendices

entries.title: Mode Inference for Substructural Adjoint Types
entries.abstract: Adjoint types [Jang et al. 2024] provide a method of mixing substructural modes (for example, linear, affine, strict, or unrestricted) in a type system while preserving the proof-theoretic and computational properties of each mode. Uses of such a system include performing compiler optimizations or providing safety guarantees on parts of a program whose modes support them, while not restricting the programmer's ability to write other code as they usually do. However, Jang et al.'s algorithmic type system is monomorphic in the modes, requiring the programmer to anticipate a potentially large number of combinations of modes, and possibly copy code to conform to each of them. In this paper we define a mode inference algorithm for programs with adjoint types that produces principal modes, summarizing all possible substructural modes of a function in a simple constraint language. This removes the burden from the programmer to a priori analyze the substructural properties of their code, and, furthermore, allows a single function definition to subsume all its instances at different modes. We show that our system is sound and complete with respect to a mild restriction of Jang et al.'s monomorphic version.

entries.title: Detecting Empty Abstractions and Pruning Dead Paths in the Linux eBPF Verifier with Abstract Step Functions
entries.abstract: The Linux kernel's eBPF verifier uses abstract interpretation to ensure the safety of user-provided programs before execution. It tracks each register with multiple interval domains and a bitwise domain (tristate numbers). Refining the abstract state at conditional branches can produce mutually contradictory constraints across domains, indicating an unreachable path. However, the verifier lacks an empty-set (⊥) representation and cannot detect when these domains have an empty intersection, causing it to analyze dead paths. Passing such contradictory states into domain reduction or downstream operators violates their implicit non-emptiness precondition, triggering domain invariant violations. This has been a multi-year issue in the Linux kernel causing production outages, false rejections, and state explosion. This paper presents a sound and complete constant-time emptiness check across the eBPF verifier's abstract domains to prune dead branches. We introduce abstract step functions, a general framework that tests whether intervals and non-convex domains intersect in O(1) time without scanning individual values. We develop tnum_step, a formally verified constant-time operator that jumps to the next integer satisfying a tristate bitmask. Using tnum_step, we design a multi-domain emptiness check that detects contradictory states during branch refinement and immediately prunes unreachable branches, eliminating the root cause of dead-branch invariant violations. Our technique prevents invariant violations, state explosion, and false rejections while incurring negligible (1.48%) overhead across Linux kernel selftests and production suites such as Cilium. Our tnum_step operator has been upstreamed into the mainline Linux kernel.

entries.title: MetaphIR: Corpus-Scale Applicability Analysis for LLVM Peephole Optimizations
entries.abstract: Peephole optimizations replace short source instruction sequences with more efficient equivalents, typically guarded by preconditions such as requiring a constant operand to be a power of two. Since every new rewrite adds maintenance burden and compile-time cost, compiler developers need to know how often real-world programs both match the source pattern and satisfy its preconditions before committing to an implementation. Existing workflows fall short: structural search over an intermediate representation (IR) corpus of 4.8 million functions ignores preconditions and therefore overcounts, whereas implementing the rewrite and recompiling the corpus yields exact counts only after paying the engineering cost, with each run of the corpus's on-demand recompilation pipeline taking a median of 47 minutes. This delay is especially limiting when generalizing a rewrite, as developers often iterate over multiple variants to trade off coverage against complexity. We introduce MetaphIR, a system pairing a domain-specific language for expressing LLVM peephole optimizations with an indexed search engine over large IR corpora. Using a syntax modeled on LLVM's C++ matchers, MetaphIR patterns augment LLVM IR with holes and Boolean preconditions over matched values. To answer queries at interactive speed, MetaphIR builds compact per-function summaries ahead of time and uses abstract interpretation over those summaries to soundly filter out functions that cannot satisfy a query's constraints. Across twenty recent peephole optimizations from LLVM's InstCombine pass, MetaphIR recovers the exact set of functions where each rewrite applies in isolation, achieving 100% precision and recall. Queries complete in a median of 1.27 seconds—a 22x speedup over a full corpus scan—enabling developers to quickly gauge an optimization's reach and generality prior to implementation.

entries.title: Trace2ST: Recovering PLC Structured Text from I/O Traces with LLM Generation and Verification
entries.abstract: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), the industrial computers that operate power and process plants, often run programs whose source code is no longer available; however, every input and output of the controller is logged continuously. This paper therefore asks whether a large language model (LLM) can recover an executable program in Structured Text (ST), the standard PLC language of IEC 61131-3, from such input/output records (traces) alone and, equally important, how the recovered program can be verified. To answer this question, we build a generate-replay-feedback pipeline. First, the LLM writes a candidate program from a compressed summary of the trace, without ever seeing the original program. The candidate is then executed one control cycle (scan) at a time and compared with the recording, and whenever a mismatch occurs the corresponding part of the trace is returned to the LLM, for at most three revisions. Because every result depends on the software that executes the candidates, we first validate it against two independent open-source PLC runtimes and find no unexplained difference. On this basis, we evaluate 47 third-party programs from two public benchmarks. The recovered programs reproduce the recorded trace exactly in 43 cases and agree with the original on 94% of scans for unseen inputs. The remaining errors, however, lie mostly in program branches that the trace never exercised; once a trace that targets these branches is added, agreement on unseen adversarial inputs rises from 0.80 to 0.98. By contrast, a classical automata-learning baseline without an LLM fits the recording but falls to 0.40 on unseen inputs, which indicates that recovering program structure is the hard part. Finally, on real data from a public water-treatment testbed, the recovered control laws match unseen measurements closely (R² > 0.99) and expose the only actuator attack in the dataset.
entries.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference (TPEC 2027)

entries.title: How well does graph superoptimization transfer? Adapting tensor-graph superoptimizer to a Triton-based NPU
entries.abstract: For automatic optimization systems, performance portability across increasingly diverse AI accelerators remains a challenge. We investigate how well graph-level superoptimization transfers across architectures by adapting Mirage from its CUDA-oriented design to the Huawei Ascend 910B3 through a Triton-based compilation stack. We evaluate the adapted system on transformer-relevant workloads, including matrix multiplication, softmax, RMSNorm+MatMul, gated MLP, FNN, and attention. The results show that graph-level optimization can successfully transfer and outperform available reference implementations by up to 87.0% on fused workloads. However, performance is highly dependent on tensor shape and workload structure, with substantial regressions for other configurations. We identify target-specific tensor partitioning, execution-resource modeling, backend lowering and fusion, and search and verification costs as key limitations. Our findings demonstrate that a portable graph representation and programming model do not imply a portable optimization space, motivating modular target-specific mechanisms within otherwise reusable compiler infrastructure.
entries.comment: Accepted for FlagOS Forum at MICRO 2026 - OASIS-AI workshop: Open Compute Architecture and Software Infrastructure for Heterogeneous AI Systems

entries.title: Statically Typed Purely Functional Definitional Interpreters for Essentials of Programming Languages
entries.abstract: Definitional interpreters provide an executable and pedagogically effective way to explain programming language semantics. However, when implemented in a dynamically typed and effectful metalanguage, semantic components such as stores, continuations, handlers, substitutions, and scheduling states may remain implicit in the host-language implementation, making it harder to see how language extensions affect interpreter structure. This paper reconstructs the family of interpreters from Essentials of Programming Languages (EOPL) in Haskell, a statically typed and purely functional metalanguage, for pedagogical use. We preserve the object languages, examples, and tests of EOPL while making their semantic components explicit through algebraic data types, evaluator signatures, and explicit semantic domains. Across 15 interpreters and 6 type checkers, language extensions are exposed as systematic type-directed changes. The reconstruction is currently used in undergraduate and graduate programming language courses, where students learn interpreter construction through incremental and test-driven development. We further illustrate its pedagogical use through three case studies that progressively extend students' experience: composing mutable state and exception handling, deriving an actor-based interpreter from the typed structure of the EOPL thread interpreter, and translating the CHECKED interpreter and type checker into Rocq to mechanize type safety. Together, the classroom experience and case studies suggest that the reconstruction provides a concrete bridge from learning programming language concepts through executable interpreters to language design and mechanized reasoning.
entries.comment: The 24th Asian Symposium on Programming Languages and Systems (APLAS 2026)

entries.title: A Unifying Metatheorem on Weak-Memory Robustness
entries.abstract: Memory models specify the behaviors that concurrent programs may exhibit under compiler and hardware optimizations, which often deviate from Sequential Consistency (SC). Robustness is the property of a program P not exhibiting any weak behaviors when executing under a weak memory model MM, compared to SC. As such, the algorithmic problem of deciding whether P is robust against MM has been studied extensively, and has been repeatedly shown to be in PSPACE for many memory models, such as TSO, PSO, and Release/Acquire. However, each model has required its own, dedicated proof, raising the natural question of whether robustness admits a unifying treatment across memory models. In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for a broad class of memory models definable in Kleene Algebra with Tests (KAT). We prove that robustness against any prefix-closed, KAT-definable memory model is in PSPACE. This metatheorem recovers nearly all prior PSPACE robustness results, and establishes PSPACE membership for several new models, including the full RC11 and the OCaml memory model. We have further formalized the correctness of our approach in Lean. On the other hand, we prove that robustness against the KAT-definable Relaxed model is undecidable, and thus prefix-closedness cannot be dropped, in general. Finally, we implement our algorithm in a prototype tool RoboKAT, and demonstrate its flexibility by checking robustness against nine memory models, several of which are not handled by prior work.

entries.title: Python Code Generation for Isabelle/HOL
entries.abstract: The Isabelle theorem prover provides an environment for formalising mathematics and reasoning about programs. To make verified implementations practically usable, its code generator translates functions expressed in the executable fragment of its logic into conventional programming languages. Its targets have traditionally been functional languages (Standard ML, OCaml, Haskell, and Scala), recently joined by Go. Python, which is becoming the dominant language of scientific computing, data science, and education, has remained out of reach. In this work, we close this gap with a Python backend for Isabelle's code generator. This generator enables verified algorithms to be used in Python applications, or to serve as verified references against which established Python libraries can be differentially tested, without leaving the Python ecosystem. We validate the backend on regression suites covering large parts of the HOL library and by testing six verified data structures and algorithms against established Python libraries. The generated code is slower than hand-written libraries, but well suited as a verified reference.
entries.comment: 20 pages, 19 figures, 2 tables. Software artefact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24106993

entries.title: Datatypes In, Zippers Out!
entries.abstract: A zipper represents a focused position in an algebraic data structure together with the context needed to reconstruct the whole. Datatype derivatives determine one-hole context types, but do not by themselves choose a zipper's concrete representation or specify navigation costs and demands. We present Kamot, a tool that converts regular algebraic datatype declarations in a restricted Haskell fragment into zipper implementations with operational contracts. Navigation, replacement, and reconstruction are proved correct against a reference traversal. Kamot supports mutual recursion and regular containers inside containers. A compositional analysis derives sound bounds on transitions and constructor demands for certified traversal directions. These bounds are affine in trail depth (the number of saved frames) and guarantee termination of each move on productive, potentially infinite inputs. For inhabited families the analysis is complete: when no move certificate is emitted, no bound depending only on trail depth exists, and some productive input makes a move diverge. We prove that the generated code preserves results and the reference order of constructor matches, including finite prefixes of divergent searches. Lean 4 verifies simulation, bounds, and completeness for finite values of single self-recursive datatypes, in both directions. On 19 datatype models and 81 generated families, every generated module passes Haskell type checking, and independent checkers validate certificates, traces, and bounds. In a prefetching workload, starting only searches whose bounds fit a budget answers every local query and avoids discarded source evaluations on long returns, but conservative bounds can lose answers that fuelled search delivers.

entries.title: SkiNet-Sim: Simulating Petri Nets with Data for the Verification and Validation of Controllers for Autonomous Systems
entries.abstract: A large amount of high-level Petri net formalisms has been investigated and deployed in academic settings over the past decades, but these deployments fail to reach practical applications, despite the strong guarantees they can bring to stakeholders. In particular, the lack of direct benefits from end-users reduces the appeal of Petri nets, both due to the overly simple classical Petri net formalism, and the overly specialized high-level formalisms, on top of state-space explosion issues. In this work, we investigate how a middle-ground could be reached, by separating the implementation-specific aspects of software or hardware behaviors, from the classical Petri net semantics. The goal is to benefit from the sought-after aspects of Petri nets, namely their simple firing semantic and model-checking capabilities, while still being able to augment their behavior to best reflect the modelled system. We present a formal model of Interpreted Petri nets with data-aware transitions and tokens. We illustrate this formalism by modelling the executive layer of a robotic system, and provide a lightweight tool to augment classical Petri nets for general purpose applications, as well as data-aware state-space exploration for model-checking. Their specialization in the context of autonomous robotics is showcased, with a complete industrial inspection mission use-case, to compare simulation and model-checking results between the classical and the new data-aware Petri net semantic.

entries.title: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty
entries.abstract: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.
entries.comment: 26 pages, 1 figure, 24 tables, including appendices. Code and reproduction artifacts at https://github.com/dqswordman/program-structure-certificates

entries.title: A Compilation Model for Divergent Parallel Workloads
entries.abstract: Efficient execution on modern parallel machines requires more than abundant parallelism; it demands instruction coherence, memory coherence, and load balance to maximize SIMD utilization and memory bandwidth. Efficiently mapping divergent parallel workloads to modern machines, where control flow, memory accesses, and unbounded iteration depend on per-thread runtime values, often requires global program restructuring that trades off increased coherence with reduced locality, parallelism, or extra work. We observe that the key optimizations used to accelerate divergent parallel programs can be expressed as compositions of well-known program transformations from the functional programming and loop optimization communities. We operationalize this insight through parallel dispatch graphs: a compilation model that represents divergent programs by representing control flow, data flow between logical stages, and parallel loops within a single abstraction. To facilitate rapid exploration of points in the optimization space, we provide a scheduling language that includes composable transformations of data-dependent control flow and data flow, together with standard loop transformations and hardware bindings. This separation of concerns allows the core algorithm to remain portable, while the execution schedule can be specialized to the specifics of target hardware and input data values. We evaluate our system using popular applications from the domain of spatial computing, and show that the optimization strategies of hand-optimized parallel tree traversals, path tracers, and Monte Carlo PDE solvers can be reproduced as schedules in our system. Our generated code matches or outperforms the hand-optimized implementations (geomeans 1.02–2.95× faster). Additionally, we demonstrate empirically that the best schedule varies across programs, machines, and inputs.

entries.title: Simulating Quantum Computation Using Probabilistic Programming
entries.abstract: Developing quantum programs requires not only running them on quantum hardware but also simulating them on classical hardware. Because the meaning of a quantum program can be defined in terms of state vectors, it can be viewed as a form of weighted nondeterminism and simulated using any implementation of probabilistic programming that supports complex or at least negative weights. In this study, we compile a high-level quantum programming language to one such implementation of probabilistic programming, a solver for factor graph grammars. We also extend the solver with an optimization that commutes the tensor operations einsum and expand. We prove that the compiler and the optimization preserve the denotational semantics of the source language. We perform benchmarks that show our straightforward implementation, by repurposing existing infrastructure for probabilistic programming, attains simulation performance in the ballpark of several other quantum simulators.

entries.title: Logical Relations on Display
entries.abstract: The metatheory of programming languages suffers from a lack of reuse. Researchers develop individual calculi and prove standard properties, but very few results are truly reused across papers. The problem is worse in proof assistants, where developments routinely duplicate code from prior work or rebuild it from scratch. Category theory provides the most promising path toward reusable programming language semantics. Universal properties capture the type connectives—products, functions, sums—together with their β/η laws. Free categorical structures identify syntactic calculi. Displayed categories provide a uniform language for specifying logical relations, and general theorems about fibrations allow their structure to be assembled compositionally. In this work we develop a library of formalized category theory in the Cubical Agda proof assistant directly applicable to programming language metatheory. We develop theories of universal properties and free categorical structures, apply them to define denotational semantics and logical relations for simply typed calculi, and identify encodings of the categorical constructions that make typechecking them tractable. From the same categorical components, we construct several familiar results via a logical relations construction—canonicity,parametricity,conservativity—and provide a proof of coherence for monoidal categories.
entries.comment: 31 pages, 3 figures, to appear at POPL 2027

entries.title: Do Apple M-Series Processors Enforce the Compound Memory Model? Sequential and Parallel Composition of Arm and TSO
entries.abstract: Apple's M-series processors can run each thread under the Arm memory model or under a TSO model, and threads of both kinds can share memory. This raises two questions of composition that Apple has not answered. Across threads, how does the machine behave as a whole? Within a thread, which Arm instructions play the roles of TSO's loads, stores and atomic read-modify-writes, and how are they ordered between themselves and across other Arm instructions? We propose that both answers are compositions of preserved program order. Across threads, each thread keeps the preserved program order of its own model: a parallel composition. Within a TSO thread, every Arm instruction keeps TSO's order and adds Arm's, and every atomic memory operation (AMO) is locked, as x86's read-modify-writes are: a sequential composition. We test both on an Apple M1 and an Apple M2 running Linux, with 936 litmus tests chosen from the two models' preserved program order, each run 6x10^8 times on each machine. Arm-mode threads follow Arm's official model, TSO-mode threads follow x86-TSO and the sequential composition, and programs that mix the two modes follow the compound model: neither machine shows an outcome these models forbid. Both machines also preserve three orders that these models do not require, and a compare-and-swap whose comparison fails behaves as if it writes back the value it read, which the Arm model does not require. All three orders held in runs up to 40 times longer.

entries.title: Agent-Native by Design: A Programming Language for Agentic Applications
entries.abstract: Building agentic applications requires combining large language model (LLM) operations, workflow structure and application state, and model-guided routing. With SDKs and agent frameworks, developers connect these components through supporting code that prepares model inputs, propagates state, and dispatches model-selected steps. Workflow changes can require coordinated updates to this code, increasing development and testing effort. Splitting execution logic between application code and framework internals also limits compiler visibility into control flow and state dependencies, hindering automatic optimization. We introduce Agent-Native Programming, which unifies these three components with shared execution semantics. We realize this approach in Jac, a Python-superset language, through "by llm()" for typed model operations and tool use, Object-Spatial Programming for workflow structure and state, and "visit... by llm()" for model-guided routing. The routing construct derives the model's choices from executable workflow steps and schedules the selected steps. This explicit connection between model decisions and program execution gives the compiler and runtime a common basis for dependency analysis and automatic optimization. Across five benchmarks and five baselines, Jac achieves a 1.8-8.7x reduction in AI-integration code relative to the OpenAI SDK, with competitive observed task quality and lower coding-agent development effort. Two case studies demonstrate speculative execution and service partitioning through configuration alone, using program analysis and runtime checks to preserve workflow behavior under stated conditions.

entries.title: Specifying & Verifying Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
entries.abstract: Building quantum computers is challenging due to the noise that affects qubits. Quantum error correction tackles noise by encoding information in quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes. These codes are often complex, increasingly found by computational search, presented in diverse formalisms with informal arguments, and hard to reason about algorithmically. Given that the rest of the quantum computing stack relies on a QEC code's properties for correct computation, we propose a formally verified foundation for QEC codes. We present QECLean, a Lean-based framework for formally specifying and verifying QEC codes. QECLean backs every claimed QEC-code property with a machine-checked proof, unifies the diverse presentations of codes in the literature through common abstractions, and makes new codes easy to specify. We present a new compositional technique, code combinators, for proving code distance analytically. Code combinators allow us to prove the distance of large codes that are out of reach for algorithmic techniques; for example, we show that IBM's [[360, 12, ≤24]] code has distance 24, which was previously only known as an upper bound. Furthermore, we show how our approach allows us to formalize and prove entire code families, such as the surface code. Our work lays the foundation required for reasoning about circuit-level implementations of codes on given architectures and for building end-to-end verified compilers for quantum computers. QECLean is available at https://github.com/Stavan-Jain/QECLean

entries.title: SAFE: Formal Specification and Implementation of a Scalable Analysis Framework for ECMAScript
entries.abstract: The prevalent uses of JavaScript in web programming have revealed security vulnerability issues of JavaScript applications, which emphasizes the need for JavaScript analyzers to detect such issues. Recently, researchers have proposed several analyzers of JavaScript programs and some web service companies have developed various JavaScript engines. However, unfortunately, most of the tools are not documented well, thus it is very hard to understand and modify them. Or, such tools are often not open to the public. In this paper, we present formal specification and implementation of SAFE, a scalable analysis framework for ECMAScript, developed for the JavaScript research community. This is the very first attempt to provide both formal specification and its opensource implementation for JavaScript, compared to the existing approaches focused on only one of them. To make it more amenable for other researchers to use our framework, we formally define three kinds of intermediate representations for JavaScript used in the framework, and we provide formal specifications of translations between them. To be adaptable for adventurous future research including modifications in the original JavaScript syntax, we actively use open-source tools to automatically generate parsers and some intermediate representations. To support a variety of program analyses in various compilation phases, we design the framework to be as flexible, scalable, and pluggable as possible. Finally, our framework is publicly available, and some collaborative research using the framework are in progress.

entries.title: CompCert4Lean: Porting a Verified C Compiler to Lean in Six Weeks with Parallel Coding Agents
entries.abstract: We present CompCert4Lean, a large-scale port of CompCert 3.17's verified compiler core from Rocq to Lean, completed in approximately six weeks by one expert directing parallel LLM agents. Our migration workflow partitions the development along its dependencies, audits translated definitions and theorem statements before large-scale proof reconstruction, and then reconstructs proofs in parallel against stable interfaces. The resulting compiler covers typed CompCert C through x86-64 assembly, discharges all 4,908 recorded proof obligations without project-specific axioms, and produces executable Linux binaries. The workflow enabled the expert to concentrate on organizing the work rather than supplying technical solutions. Of 1,071 human interactions, 88.8% concerned workflow and coordination, while only three supplied technical direction. Optimization campaigns further demonstrate the benefit of the Lean port for agent-driven verified development. Under matched budgets of 24 active hours, GPT-6-astra produced a Lean candidate with 11.7% lower generated-program runtime across 29 small-tests programs, compared with 2.3% lower for its Rocq candidate, both relative to original CompCert 3.17 and while preserving the end-to-end correctness theorem. These results show that parallel LLM agents can support large-scale migration with limited human technical direction and subsequently improve the migrated compiler while retaining its formal guarantees.

entries.title: Underpinning Property-Based Testing
entries.abstract: As the property-based testing community strives to automate challenging parts of the process away from users — in particular, the construction of generators — it is critical that we can clearly state what it means for that automation to be correct. We present a new framework for PBT, implemented in the Lean theorem prover, that provides a more solid foundation to build on. Our generators are interpretable: interpreted one way, they can be run efficiently as programs that sample randomness; and interpreted another way, they enable a wide range of correctness proofs, including proofs about distributions that other foundational PBT models do not support. We evaluate our framework extensively, with both small and large benchmarks and case studies, arguing that the extra power brought by distributional proofs is practically important for the next generation of generator automation.

entries.title: From Strong Normalization to WhatsApp: the Journey of an Axiom
entries.abstract: Twenty years ago, Mariangiola Dezani-Ciancaglini, Daniele Varacca and I showed that Milner's classic encoding of functions into processes does not respect one of the laws of intersection types, the one stating that (σ→τ)∧(σ→ρ) is a subtype of σ→(τ∧ρ), which Barendregt, Coppo and Dezani-Ciancaglini had stated in 1983 for their filter λ-model. In this essay I show that this observation is the key to closing what a colleague at Meta calls “the main typing gap in Erlang”—the language in which the servers of WhatsApp are written: the type of the function that implements a server is not related to the type of the server, so that a client may expect from the server a reply that the server will never send. Actually, closing this gap is just an excuse to follow the journey of the law above, and of some of its relatives, from the study of strong normalization in the λ-calculus to the type systems of Elixir and Erlang: a journey that shows how much the practical typing of these languages owes to the work of Mario Coppo, Mariangiola Dezani-Ciancaglini and Simona Ronchi Della Rocca, to whom this essay is dedicated for their eightieth birthdays.
entries.comment: Dedicated to Mario Coppo, Mariangiola Dezani-Ciancaglini, and Simona Ronchi Della Rocca, for their eightieth birthdays

entries.title: CIRT: Calculus of Inductive Refinement Types
entries.abstract: Refinement types are a powerful mechanism for statically verifying properties of programs. They have been successfully integrated into practical languages such as Haskell, Scala, and Rust. However, their metatheory is not yet fully understood. In this paper we present the first semantic model for a refinement type system that supports the full feature combination of subtyping, SMT-style equality, impredicative polymorphism, and (stratified) inductive types. Interactions between these features have led to inconsistencies in the past, and existing formalizations of refinement type systems omit at least one of them. We present a realizability model based on partial equivalence relations (PERs) over a Scott domain, which overcomes these obstacles. We use our model to prove the consistency of a core refinement type system and to give a semantic account of the annotation-independence property of refinement types. Our semantics uses two interpretations: a refined one, which interprets types and their refinements as PERs; and an unrefined one, consisting of complete uniform PERs with a bottom element (CUPERs), which models computational behaviour independently of refinements. We extend the model to positive and stratified inductive types, showing that both are consistent in the presence of impredicativity.
entries.comment: Extended version of the POPL 2027 paper

entries.title: Partial Borrows in Rust
entries.abstract: Rust ensures memory safety by requiring exclusive access to mutably borrowed data. However, a borrow can prevent access to more data than necessary. For example, a method with an &mut self parameter borrows the entire struct, even when the method uses only some of its fields. Calling the method can therefore conflict with an existing borrow of a field the method never uses, causing Rust to reject the program. Resolving such conflicts can require programmers to compromise useful abstractions, make non-local changes to their programs, or worse, resort to unsafe code. We introduce view types, a backward-compatible refinement of reference types that specifies which fields a reference may access. This allows methods to partially borrow a struct, accessing only the fields they need without blocking access to the rest. We establish the first fully mechanized foundation for Aeneas in Rocq. Along the way, we uncover and fix gaps in the original semantics and proofs. Building on this foundation, we formalize partial borrows and prove the extended borrow checking sound. We implement view types in rustc and extend the Aeneas interpreter to support partial borrows. Our evaluation shows how view types systematically resolve borrowing conflicts across method boundaries at no runtime cost.

entries.title: Strict Capabilities with a PNVI Escape Hatch
entries.abstract: Capability systems enforce memory safety by tying pointers to their originating allocations, preventing forgery, use-after-free, and out-of-bounds accesses. Yet conventional capabilities are simultaneously too strict and not strict enough for C: they reject common low-level idioms involving integer casts or raw pointer bytes, while failing to enforce type correctness and sub-object bounds. Proposed Provenance Not Via Integers (PNVI) semantics expose this tension by permitting representation-level manipulation while retaining strict rules for ordinary pointer operations. We argue that these requirements call for two interoperable abstractions rather than a compromise within one. Strict capabilities enforce provenance, liveness, type correctness, and (sub-)object bounds; ordinary capability operations preserve these invariants. Exposed representations are non-dereferenceable, integer-like values that support arbitrary integer and byte-level manipulation under PNVI semantics while retaining unforgeability guarantees. They carry no directly usable memory-access authority: converting an exposed representation back to a strict capability reconstructs provenance under PNVI rules and validates type and bounds before access. Thus, low-level C idioms can use an explicit escape hatch without weakening ordinary capability derivation. We realize this design using Fully Randomized Pointers (FRP) and dynamic type metadata. Evaluation on low-level pointer idioms, Juliet tests, and existing C benchmarks shows that strict type and sub-object safety can coexist with low-level pointer manipulation.

entries.title: Taint Analysis via Heap-Aware Propagation
entries.abstract: Taint analysis for C depends on how precisely the analysis tracks tainted values as they flow through memory objects. Without field sensitivity, a tainted object field can spuriously taint an entire object, producing significant false alarms. In this paper, we present a field-sensitive taint analysis that combines Data Structure Analysis (DSA) for field-sensitive points-to information with a data-flow analysis for tracking explicit dependencies. We identify that existing DSA-style analyses lose precision on a common object pattern: a C struct object that mixes scalar fields with a flexible array member. When such an array is accessed with symbolic indices, DSA loses points-to field sensitivity for the entire object, inflating false alarms in the data-flow analysis. To address this, we propose I-DSA, which extends DSA by representing field positions as intervals, so that a pointer with symbolic bounds merges only the fields within those bounds. We further develop a sound data-flow analysis based on abstract interpretation. We implement I-DSA on top of SeaDSA and the data-flow analysis inside Crab. Our tool targets LLVM IR and supports configurable taint policies by instrumenting the IR with taint intrinsics. Our experiments show that I-DSA reduces the false alarms caused by this pattern at little cost in the pointer analysis, that SVF, an inclusion-based pointer analysis, shows a similar field-sensitivity loss, and that our taint analysis scales better than PhASAR on real-world programs.
entries.comment: This is an extended version of the VMCAI 2027 paper, consisting of 31 pages. The artifact is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19826762

entries.title: Type-Confusion Security
entries.abstract: Type systems are a lightweight way to obtain formal assurance that code upholds security properties. However, decentralized systems, such as smart contracts and Model Context Protocol ecosystems, have limited ability to constrain the behavior of untrusted code. In such systems, attackers may attempt to confuse trusted code by supplying values that do not behave according to their advertised types, an attack that we call type confusion. Well-known attacks such as confused deputy attacks, reentrancy attacks, and control-flow hijacking can be understood as instances of type confusion. We define type confusion security as the property that unrestricted attackers who need not follow the type system have no more power than limited attackers who fully obey it. We formally define type confusion security as a real–ideal emulation, and in the context of an information-flow-typed core calculus that statically enforces security against well-typed attackers, prove that its run-time checks also enforce security against ill-typed attackers. In this system, programmers can write code while reasoning about security only against well-typed attackers; the security guarantees enforced by the type system still hold. We mechanize a proof of type confusion security in Lean.
entries.comment: The first two authors contributed equally to this work

entries.title: GraphPass: A Study of Graph Neural Networks for Compiler Pass Selection
entries.abstract: Compiler pass selection is usually governed by fixed pipelines (-O2, -O3) or hand-written heuristics. We study whether a graph neural network (GNN) over a program's control-flow graph (CFG) can select among a fixed menu of five pass sequences in a single forward pass. GraphPass encodes each CFG with a graph attention (GAT) or graph convolutional (GCN) encoder and classifies it into one of the five sequences. On a synthetic benchmark of 5,000 generated CFGs in five program families, both encoders agree with the benchmark's reference label on about 92% of held-out programs, versus 68.4% for a hand-written rule-based heuristic and 85% for a flat MLP. An edge ablation indicates that this gain comes from per-block processing rather than from CFG edges: a GCN given the same basic-block features with all edges removed scores 95.0%, versus 92.2% with the true CFG. In this benchmark the label is determined by the program family, so the task amounts to family recognition. Real-compiler speedup is not measured. Inference costs O(|V| + |E|) per CFG, measured at 1.7 ms for a typical program and about 0.8 s for a 100,000-block graph on one CPU core.

entries.title: Proxima: Optimizing Syndrome Extraction Circuit Scheduling for Practical Quantum LDPC Codes
entries.abstract: The fault-tolerant performance of quantum error correction codes relies critically on the scheduling of parity checks in syndrome extraction circuits (SECs). For general CSS-type quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, the vast scheduling space and intricate error-propagation patterns make it computationally prohibitive to directly optimize the logical error rate (LER) or the exact circuit-level distance (d_circ). To address this challenge, we introduce Proxima, a highly effective automated SEC scheduling framework guided by a distance-related metric termed proximity. Defined directly on the detector error model (DEM), proximity quantifies the minimum number of additional faults required to complete a seed fault to an undetectable logical failure, naturally capturing arbitrary circuit-level fault mechanisms and bounding d_circ from above. Proxima synthesizes a pool of valid schedules at a target depth and ranks them by evaluating proximity within small, graph-local DEM fault subsets, progressively enlarging the subset only to break ties among top-ranked candidates. Across a broad spectrum of qLDPC code families, Proxima consistently attains low circuit depths and high circuit-level distance bounds, reducing LER by 1.4–2.6× over the strongest automated baseline and up to 40× over others while generalizing robustly across noise models and decoders. Furthermore, by exploiting translational symmetry via a compact monomial representation, Proxima discovers depth-8 uniform schedules for bivariate bicycle codes that surpass even IBM's depth-7 reference schedule [Nature, 2024] by 2.1–5.1×, establishing the DEM-level proximity as a practical objective for fault-tolerant compilation.

entries.title: Latency-Preserving Rewrites and Translation Validation for Dynamic Quantum Circuits
entries.abstract: A dynamic quantum circuit measures qubits during a run and chooses later operations from the outcomes. These branches make the qubits wait: the outcome must reach the classical controller, and the controller must decide. We present qlin, a compiler that reduces this waiting time. qlin moves operations out of branches without delaying the program, a property proved in Lean 4. For error-correction decoders, which branch on syndromes that are almost always zero, qlin compiles the likely syndromes into one multiway branch and keeps the original program for the rest. A cost model decides when a classically controlled gate should become a quantum-controlled gate instead. On all benchmarks, qlin checks that the compiled program computes what its source computes, and the checker is proved sound in Lean 4. At the published per-decision cost of the QICK controller (42 ns), 10 of 65 programs run at least 10% faster than the best baseline in our cost model, up to 91.2%, mostly because one multiway branch replaces a long chain of if statements. On the register-transfer logic of the QubiC controller, a compiled distance-5 repetition decoder selects its correction in 21.3 instead of 151.1 expected cycles. Timing runs on an IBM device were too noisy to confirm or reject the model's ranking.

entries.title: ElevatorII: High-Performance Fully-Static Cross-ISA Binary Translation
entries.abstract: The established method for running software compiled for one instruction-set architecture (ISA) on a different ISA is by emulation in conjunction with just-in-time (JIT) compilation. This requires run-time support on the target that needs to be trusted and whose compilation decisions are hard to predict or reconstruct. We present ElevatorII, a fully static, ahead-of-time cross-ISA binary-to-binary compiler from x86 to AArch64 that challenges the established consensus. Our approach eliminates the need for run-time support on the target, removes the hard to reproduce effects of dynamic compilation, and provides the capability to exhaustively test the actual binary that is eventually executed. Our approach combines superset disassembly with observation-guided path selection. Superset disassembly overcomes the code vs. data differentiation problem by creating a separate control flow path for every possible interpretation of every byte in the input binary. It guarantees that there is pre-translated code for every possible jump destination in the original text segment, even for computed jumps that are not statically decidable. Static and observation-guided path selection then creates additional optimized "confirmed code paths" that overlay the regular grid. On the 11 SPEC CPU 2026 Integer benchmarks that do not use C++ exceptions, ElevatorII runs at 2.5x native AArch64 time, on par with Box64, the fastest dynamic translator, and 5x faster than QEMU. It also translates binaries obfuscated with virtualization and branch functions, which no static disassembler can follow. Our approach trades execution performance for space: our output code is 51x the size of code compiled from source. We alleviate this by separating cold code to a.text.unlikely ELF section: only 2-3% hot code winds up in the main ELF section, while the rest will likely never be loaded into memory.

entries.title: Compiling Imperative Hardware Protocol Specifications to Hardware
entries.abstract: Correct modular composition in hardware depends on interfaces with subtle multi-cycle timing behavior, yet such protocols remain difficult to specify, test, and debug. Recent work has demonstrated that hardware communication specifications can take the form of compact imperative programs that describe the cycle-by-cycle behavior of each logical transaction. However, prior tools only use these specifications for simulation-based testing and debugging, and their semantics remain informal. In this work, we develop a theory of hardware protocol specifications using automata. In addition to making the specifications' meaning precise, the automaton representation lets us compile them into synthesizable hardware. We implement a compiler that produces RTL modules for driving hardware interfaces and for reconstructing logical transactions from low-level I/O signals. We demonstrate a variety of use cases for synthesizable protocol drivers and reconstructors, including runtime monitors that check security properties in the Wishbone protocol and a binding generator that synthesizes interfaces between RTL modules and programs in the Calyx intermediate language.

entries.title: Formalizing einsum with Named Tensor Notation
entries.abstract: Einstein notation (einsum) is a widely adopted tensor operation that has proven useful in areas such as machine learning and quantum computing. But it had no formal semantics until recently, and its properties had no mechanized verification. We formalize the denotational semantics of a language of tensors (multi-dimensional arrays) that supports einsum and repeated tensors (expand). With this semantics, we verify equational rewriting rules about einsum and expand that improve the performance of tensor computation. Whereas typical languages use unnamed tensors, whose shape is a sequence of natural numbers, we found it advantageous for mechanization to use named tensors, whose shape is a finite map from names to natural numbers. To our knowledge, this is the first time that the semantics and rewriting rules of einsum are mechanized in a proof assistant. Our solution is agnostic to proof assistants; we have implemented it in Lean and partially in Agda.

entries.title: Executable Archaeology: Reanimating the Logic Theorist
entries.abstract: The Logic Theorist (LT), created by Allen Newell, J. C. Shaw, and Herbert Simon in 1955–1956, is regarded by some as the first artificial intelligence program. It was originally simulated by hand and written in a pseudocode called the Logic Language (LL), which was later called Information Processing Language One (IPL-I). LT was revised many times. The first machine-executed version was written in IPL-II and ran on the JOHNNIAC, and a late version was published in 1963 by Einar Stefferud as a pedagogical document and written in IPL-V, the only version of IPL that was formally released to the public. We describe a reanimation of both the IPL-I (LL) version of LT and the 1963 IPL-V version. Comparing the two reanimations illuminates the process of the invention of early AI algorithms and computer languages.
entries.comment: This paper builds upon a previous ArXiv paper of a similar name: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.13514. This paper is NOT a mere rehash of the previous paper; appropriate citations and comparison are provided in the discussion. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

entries.title: A Nonlinear Abstract Domain for Bayesian Neural Networks
entries.abstract: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) explicitly model epistemic uncertainty by leveraging probability distributions over network parameters, making them better suited for risk-aware decision-making. Yet soundly propagating uncertainty through the network and capturing the entire output distribution to support predictive uncertainty quantification remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches are either sampling-based, providing no formal guarantees, or propagate only selected statistical properties, such as expectations and entropy, limiting their applicability to general probabilistic queries. To address these challenges, we present the first nonlinear abstract domain for soundly approximating complete probability distributions of BNNs. The abstract domain builds upon a novel marginal collecting concrete semantics that soundly abstracts the classical joint-measure semantics. It combines support partitioning with exponential-affine bounds to represent probability measures, capturing both discrete and continuous components of mixed distributions as well as nonlinear density shapes over bounded and unbounded supports. We develop sound abstract transformers that can efficiently handle high-dimensional affine transformations and nonlinear ReLU activations, while remaining highly parallelizable. We further extend the framework beyond BNNs to support bounded-loop probabilistic programs with Bayesian inference to demonstrate its generality. We implement the resulting abstract interpreter as a GPU-accelerated analyzer. Experimental results show that the framework significantly improves precision over existing probabilistic reasoning approaches while soundly capturing the complete output distribution, demonstrating strong efficiency and scalability.

entries.title: Composable Rewrites for Layouts of Algebraic Data Types
entries.abstract: Algebraic data types (ADTs) decouple the logical structure of data from physical layout choices that affect performance. For example, packing small fields into a word improves spatial locality, while storing co-accessed fields contiguously can enable vectorization. Such choices reinforce or undermine one another, with ramifications for compiler optimizations and memory management. Their interplay creates a combinatorial space of layouts with different runtime costs and memory footprints. The most favorable layout depends on the program's construction and destruction patterns, the characteristics of input data, and the target machine. Exploring this space requires control over layout decisions and a way to compose them while preserving program semantics. We provide both through rewrite rules over layouts, independent of any particular source language or bit-level encoding. Starting from a canonical layout derived from the ADT, these rules transform its representation while leaving the source program intact. We identify a local refinement criterion for proving each rewrite rule correct, so that layouts continue to represent every value and keep distinct values apart. Adding a new rule therefore only requires a proof satisfying this local criterion. We realize these rules in Isomer, a new pure functional programming language whose compiler specializes construction, pattern matching, and memory management to the chosen layouts. Using a default layout for all ADTs, Isomer achieves competitive performance against established functional compilers that automatically select layouts. Our rewrites further improve performance by tailoring layouts to each workload, permitting representations that prior work cannot attain or can only achieve through explicit changes to the source code.
